title: CCNA Exam Preparation: Practice Labs and Review
subtitle: Review all six CCNA (200-301) domains with Packet Tracer practice labs, learn a structured troubleshooting method, and prove your skills on a multi-site network you build and then fix.
outcomes: Plan your CCNA study around the exam's six domains and Cisco's published topics
Subnet IPv4 networks quickly and work confidently with IPv6 addresses
Build and verify VLANs, trunks, inter-VLAN routing, EtherChannel and Rapid PVST+
Configure and verify static routes and single-area OSPFv2, and read any routing table
Review IP services, security and automation topics with the exam's traps in mind
Troubleshoot networks with a structured method, layer by layer
prerequisites: You should already have studied the CCNA topics: this course reviews and practises them rather than teaching them from the beginning. Install Cisco Packet Tracer (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account) on Windows, macOS or Linux.
description:
This course is the last stage before the CCNA (200-301) exam: a structured review of all six domains in Cisco's published exam topics, built around practice in Cisco Packet Tracer. It starts with the exam itself, what it covers and how to prepare efficiently, and with a troubleshooting method you'll use in every lab. Then three review modules cover the domains in groups: network fundamentals and network access, with fast subnetting, IPv6, VLANs, trunks, EtherChannel and Rapid PVST+; IP connectivity, with routing tables, static routes and single-area OSPFv2; and IP services, security fundamentals and automation, reviewed with the exam's favourite traps in mind.

Each review module ends with a practice lab in two halves: build and verify a working network, then paste in a colleague's faulty change and use the method to find and fix every fault. The capstone puts it all together in a head office and branch network that you build, break and troubleshoot back to health, with a log of every fault. The course is independent of Cisco and is meant to sit alongside Cisco's own exam topics and preparation materials.
aligned_with: Cisco CCNA (200-301) exam topics: all six domains

modules.title: Plan your preparation, and troubleshoot with a method
modules.summary: What the exam covers and how to prepare for it, how to practise efficiently in Packet Tracer, and the structured troubleshooting method used in every lab that follows.

lessons.title: The six domains and the exam topics
objectives: Name the six domains of the CCNA (200-301) exam topics
Use the published exam topics as a study checklist
key_points: Cisco's CCNA (200-301) exam topics are grouped into six domains: Network Fundamentals, Network Access, IP Connectivity, IP Services, Security Fundamentals, and Automation and Programmability.

Cisco publishes a percentage weight for each domain. IP Connectivity has carried the most, followed by Network Fundamentals and Network Access, so addressing, switching and routing deserve the most practice. Check the current list on Cisco's site when you plan.

Each topic starts with a verb that says how deeply it's tested, such as describe, explain, compare, interpret, or configure and verify. Configure-and-verify topics need hands-on practice, not just reading.
Questions can be multiple choice with one or several answers, drag and drop, and simulations or simlets, in which you work on a simulated device or read output from one.
The exam is timed and you can't go back to a question once you've moved on, so answer each one as well as you can before you leave it.
Passing earns the CCNA certification, which is valid for three years; you renew it by passing an exam again or by earning continuing education credits.

lessons.title: How to study: recall, spacing and practice labs
objectives: Build a study plan around active recall and spaced review
Practise efficiently in Packet Tracer and the IOS command line
key_points: Active recall, answering questions from memory, builds longer-lasting knowledge than rereading notes, and spaced review, returning to a topic after days and then weeks, keeps it.
Practise every configure-and-verify topic on devices: type the commands, then prove the result with show commands. Knowing what correct output looks like is half of every troubleshooting question.
Drill subnetting until it's quick and automatic: questions about routing, ACLs and addressing all depend on it.
Keep an error log of every question or lab you get wrong, why, and the fact you were missing, and read it before each study session.
In the IOS command line, ? lists what can come next, Tab completes a word, do runs a show command from configuration mode, and | include or | begin filters long output.
Take timed practice tests late in your preparation to find your weak domains, then go back to labs for those domains.

steps.do: Build a practice topology you can reuse: two 2911 routers, two 2960 switches and two PCs, cabled. Save it as practice-base.pkt, so every drill starts from it in seconds.
On a router's CLI tab, ask for help partway through a command.
steps.code: show ip ?
steps.see: Everything that can follow show ip, each with a short description.

steps.do: Run a show command without leaving configuration mode by putting do in front of it.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface g0/0
 do show ip interface brief

steps.do: Filter long output to the part you need.
steps.code:
end
show running-config | include interface
show running-config | begin line vty
steps.see: Only the lines that match, or everything from the first match on.

steps.do: Watch a ping travel: switch to Simulation mode, pick the Add Simple PDU tool (the closed envelope), click a PC and then the other PC, and step through with Capture/Forward.
steps.see: The packet moving hop by hop, with each device's view in the Event List.

steps.do: After each drill, save a copy of the finished lab with its date, so you can compare your next attempt with it.

lessons.title: A structured troubleshooting method
objectives: Follow a structured process from symptom to documented fix
Choose between bottom-up, top-down, divide-and-conquer and follow-the-path
key_points: A structured process stops you guessing: define the problem, gather information, analyse it, eliminate possible causes, propose the most likely one, test it with one change, and once it's solved, document the cause and the fix.

Bottom-up starts at the physical layer and works up, which suits problems that look physical; top-down starts at the application, which suits one failing application. Divide-and-conquer starts in the middle, often with a ping, and goes up or down from the result.
Follow-the-path traces the route traffic takes from source to destination, checking each device on the way; comparing with a known-good configuration or a baseline shows what changed.
Change one thing at a time and test after each change. If a change doesn't fix the problem, undo it, so you don't add new faults.

ping tests reachability and traceroute shows where traffic stops; show commands then narrow the cause layer by layer: show interfaces, then show vlan brief and show interfaces trunk, then show ip route and show ip protocols.
A baseline recorded while the network works (interface counters, routing tables, neighbours and utilisation) turns 'is this normal?' into a quick comparison.

walkthrough.title: Follow the path from symptom to cause

steps.do: A user on PC1 can't reach a server at 192.168.30.10. Define the problem precisely by testing it yourself from PC1.
Divide and conquer: ping PC1's own gateway. If that fails, the problem is local to PC1's LAN; if it works, follow the path beyond it.
See where along the path traffic stops.
steps.see: Each router that answers, then asterisks from the point where traffic is lost.

steps.do: On the last router that answered, check its route to the destination and the state of the interface it would use.
steps.code:
show ip route 192.168.30.10
show ip interface brief
steps.see: Either no route that matches, so the routing table is the problem, or a route out of an interface that's down, so the link is.

steps.do: Make one change, repeat the same ping from PC1, and write down the symptom, the cause and the fix.

modules.title: Review: Network Fundamentals and Network Access
modules.summary: Addressing at speed, then switching: VLANs, trunks, inter-VLAN routing, EtherChannel and Rapid PVST+, with a practice lab that ends in a fault to find.

lessons.title: IPv4 subnetting and IPv6 addressing at speed
objectives: Work out a subnet's network, broadcast and host range in your head
Shorten IPv6 addresses and recognise their types
key_points: Subtract the mask's interesting octet from 256 to get the block size: a /27 (255.255.255.224) has blocks of 32, so 192.168.1.77/27 is in 192.168.1.64, with broadcast 192.168.1.95 and hosts .65 to .94.
A subnet with h host bits has 2^h - 2 usable addresses: a /24 has 254, a /26 62, a /28 14 and a /30 2. A /31 has no network or broadcast address and suits point-to-point links (RFC 3021).
With VLSM each subnet gets the size it needs: allocate the largest subnets first, from the start of the range, so the smaller ones fit after them without overlapping.

An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits. Leading zeros in a group can be dropped, and one run of all-zero groups can become :: (once only): 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 is 2001:db8::1.
IPv6 address types: global unicast (2000::/3), link-local (fe80::/10, on every IPv6 interface and never routed), unique local (fc00::/7) and multicast (ff00::/8). IPv6 has no broadcast.

With EUI-64, an interface builds its 64-bit interface ID from its 48-bit MAC address by inserting FFFE in the middle and flipping the seventh bit; with SLAAC, hosts build their own addresses from the prefix routers advertise.

walkthrough.title: Configure and check IPv6 on a router

steps.do: On R1, turn on IPv6 routing, give g0/0 a global address, and let g0/1 build its own with EUI-64.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ipv6 unicast-routing
interface g0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:10::1/64
 no shutdown
 exit
interface g0/1
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 eui-64
 no shutdown
 end

steps.do: Check the addresses.
steps.code: show ipv6 interface brief
steps.see: Each interface with a link-local address starting FE80:: and its global address; g0/1's ends in an interface ID made from its MAC address, with FFFE in the middle.

steps.do: On a PC in g0/0's LAN, open Desktop | IP Configuration and choose Automatic under IPv6 Configuration.
steps.see: An address in 2001:db8:acad:10::/64 built by SLAAC, and R1's link-local address as the IPv6 gateway.

steps.do: Ping R1's global address from the PC.
steps.code: ping 2001:db8:acad:10::1
steps.see: Replies from 2001:db8:acad:10::1.

lessons.title: VLANs, trunks and inter-VLAN routing
objectives: Configure VLANs, access ports and 802.1Q trunks, and verify them
Route between VLANs with a router on a stick
key_points: A VLAN is a separate broadcast domain on a switch. An access port belongs to one VLAN (switchport access vlan 10), and every port starts in VLAN 1, the default.

An 802.1Q trunk carries many VLANs on one link by adding a 4-byte tag with the VLAN ID to each frame, except frames in the native VLAN (VLAN 1 unless changed), which travel untagged. The native VLAN must match at both ends.

switchport mode trunk makes a trunk, switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99 limits the VLANs it carries, and switchport trunk native vlan 99 changes the native VLAN; switchport nonegotiate turns off DTP negotiation.

A router on a stick routes between VLANs over one trunk: one subinterface per VLAN, such as g0/0.10 with encapsulation dot1Q 10 and the VLAN's gateway address. A Layer 3 switch does the same with SVIs and ip routing.
show vlan brief lists the VLANs and their access ports (trunk ports aren't listed), and show interfaces trunk lists each trunk with its native VLAN and the VLANs allowed and active on it.
Common faults: an access port in the wrong VLAN, a VLAN missing from a trunk's allowed list, a native VLAN mismatch, and a subinterface with the wrong VLAN number.

walkthrough.title: Build two VLANs and route between them

steps.do: On S1, create the VLANs and put the PCs' ports in them.
steps.code:
configure terminal
vlan 10
 name Staff
vlan 20
 name Guest
vlan 99
 name Management
 exit
interface f0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 exit
interface f0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 exit

steps.do: Make the link to the router a trunk with native VLAN 99.
steps.code:
interface g0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
 end

steps.do: On R1, create a subinterface for each VLAN, and bring up the physical interface.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface g0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 exit
interface g0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 exit
interface g0/0.99
 encapsulation dot1Q 99 native
 ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0
 exit
interface g0/0
 no shutdown
 end

steps.do: Check the switch's side.
steps.code:
show vlan brief
show interfaces trunk
steps.see: Fa0/1 in VLAN 10 and Fa0/2 in VLAN 20, and Gig0/1 trunking with native VLAN 99.

steps.do: Ping the VLAN 20 PC from the VLAN 10 PC.
steps.see: Replies: R1 routes between the VLANs.

lessons.title: EtherChannel and Rapid PVST+
objectives: Bundle links with LACP and verify the EtherChannel
Interpret Rapid PVST+ root election, port roles and PortFast
key_points: EtherChannel bundles parallel links into one logical port-channel, adding bandwidth without spanning tree blocking any of them. LACP, the IEEE standard, has active and passive modes; Cisco's PAgP has desirable and auto; mode on forms a channel without negotiating.
A channel forms only when the ports match (speed, duplex and VLAN or trunk settings) and the modes are compatible: passive with passive, or auto with auto, never forms one.

Spanning tree elects one root bridge per VLAN: the lowest bridge ID, which is the priority (32768 by default, plus the VLAN number) followed by the MAC address. spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary makes a switch win.

Every other switch picks one root port, its lowest-cost path to the root; each segment has one designated port; the remaining ports become alternate or backup ports and discard frames, which breaks loops.
Rapid PVST+ ports are discarding, learning or forwarding. PortFast takes an access port to an end device straight to forwarding, and BPDU guard err-disables that port if a switch is plugged into it.

show etherchannel summary shows each bundle and its ports, (SU) for a Layer 2 channel in use and (P) for each bundled port; show spanning-tree vlan 10 shows the root, each port's role and state, and This bridge is the root on the root.

walkthrough.title: Bundle two links and choose the root bridge

steps.do: On S1, bundle f0/23 and f0/24 with LACP and make the bundle a trunk. On S2, do the same with mode passive.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface range f0/23 - 24
 channel-group 1 mode active
 exit
interface port-channel 1
 switchport mode trunk
 end

steps.do: Check the bundle.
steps.code: show etherchannel summary
steps.see: Po1(SU) using LACP, with Fa0/23(P) and Fa0/24(P).

steps.do: Use Rapid PVST+ on both switches, and make S1 the root bridge for VLANs 10 and 20.
steps.code:
configure terminal
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10,20 root primary
end

steps.do: Read the result on each switch.
steps.code: show spanning-tree vlan 10
steps.see: This bridge is the root on S1; on S2, Po1 is the root port.

steps.do: On the access ports to PCs, turn on PortFast and BPDU guard.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface range f0/1 - 2
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 end

lab.title: Build and fix a switched campus block
lab.goal: Build two switches with three VLANs, an LACP EtherChannel trunk, Rapid PVST+ and a router on a stick, prove it works, then find and fix the faults a colleague's change introduced.
setup: Cisco Packet Tracer 8 or later (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account)
The starter files r1-base.txt, s1-base.txt and s2-base.txt, the plan in addressing.txt, and change-s2.txt for the ticket at the end

steps.do: Build the topology in addressing.txt: R1 (2911), S1 and S2 (2960s) joined by two cables (f0/23 and f0/24), and PC1 to PC4. Paste the starter files and give the PCs their static addresses.
On both switches, create VLANs 10, 20 and 99, put the PC ports in their VLANs, and turn on PortFast and BPDU guard on them.
steps.code:
configure terminal
vlan 10
 name Staff
vlan 20
 name Guest
vlan 99
 name Management
 exit
interface f0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 exit
interface f0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 end

steps.do: Bundle f0/23-24 with LACP and make the bundle a trunk with native VLAN 99. The commands below are S1's, including g0/1, its trunk to R1; on S2, use channel-group 1 mode passive and leave out g0/1.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface range f0/23 - 24
 channel-group 1 mode active
 exit
interface port-channel 1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
 exit
interface g0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
 end

steps.do: On S1, run Rapid PVST+, make it the root for all three VLANs, and give it its management address and gateway. On S2, use spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst only, with the management address 192.168.99.3 and the same gateway.
steps.code:
configure terminal
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99 root primary
interface vlan 99
 ip address 192.168.99.2 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
ip default-gateway 192.168.99.1
end

steps.do: On R1, create the subinterfaces g0/0.10, g0/0.20 and g0/0.99 (native) with the gateway addresses in addressing.txt.
Verify the switching on S1.
steps.code:
show etherchannel summary
show interfaces trunk
show spanning-tree vlan 10
steps.see: Po1(SU) with LACP and both ports (P), Po1 and Gig0/1 trunking with native VLAN 99, and This bridge is the root.

steps.do: From PC1, ping PC3 (same VLAN, across the EtherChannel) and PC4 (another VLAN, through R1).
steps.see: Replies from both.

steps.do: The ticket: paste change-s2.txt into S2. Users report that PC3 can't reach anything. Use the troubleshooting method to find every fault and fix it, recording the commands that showed you each one.

checks.text: The EtherChannel is up, negotiated by LACP, with both ports bundled.
The trunks carry the VLANs with native VLAN 99.
S1 is the root bridge for VLAN 10.
Hosts reach each other in the same VLAN across the EtherChannel and between VLANs through R1.
The ticket is solved: PC3's port is back in VLAN 10 and VLAN 10 is allowed on S2's trunk again, each found with a show command.

lab.submit: Paste show etherchannel summary, show interfaces trunk and show spanning-tree vlan 10 from S1, PC1's two pings, and your ticket notes: each fault, the command output that revealed it, and the fix.

enable
configure terminal
interface f0/1
 switchport access vlan 20

interface port-channel 1

hints: If the EtherChannel won't form, compare the two ends with show etherchannel summary and show interfaces port-channel 1: modes, speed and trunk settings must match.
show vlan brief doesn't list trunk ports, so a PC port missing from its VLAN's line is a clue.
There are two faults in the ticket: fixing one isn't enough.

modules.title: Review: IP Connectivity
modules.summary: Read routing tables the way the exam does, configure static, default and floating routes, and run single-area OSPFv2, with a practice lab across three sites that ends in a fault to find.

lessons.title: Reading the routing table
objectives: Interpret every part of a routing table entry
Predict which route a router will use for a destination
key_points: Each entry shows how the route was learned (C connected, L local, S static, O OSPF, D EIGRP, R RIP, B BGP, with * marking a candidate default), the prefix, [administrative distance/metric], the next hop, the route's age and the exit interface.
The router forwards by longest prefix match: the most specific route containing the destination wins, so 10.1.1.0/24 beats 10.1.0.0/16, which beats 0.0.0.0/0.
When different sources offer the same prefix, the lowest administrative distance wins: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, external EIGRP 170 and iBGP 200.
When one protocol offers several routes to the same prefix, the lowest metric wins; OSPF shares the load across paths with equal cost.
The gateway of last resort is the default route's next hop. Without one, a packet that matches no route is dropped.
show ip route lists every route, show ip route 192.168.30.10 shows the route used for one address, and traceroute confirms the path traffic takes.

walkthrough.title: Read a routing table entry by entry

steps.do: On R2 in the lab network, once OSPF is running, show the routing table.
steps.code: show ip route
steps.see: The codes, Gateway of last resort is 10.0.12.1, C and L entries for each connected interface, O entries from OSPF and O*E2 for the default route.

steps.do: Read the O entry for 192.168.30.0/24: in [110/20], 110 is OSPF's administrative distance and 20 the total cost (10 for each gigabit interface on the way, with the lab's reference bandwidth); via 10.0.23.2 is the next hop, followed by the age and the exit interface.
Ask which route serves a single address.
steps.code: show ip route 192.168.30.10
steps.see: The matching prefix 192.168.30.0/24, how it was learned, its distance and metric, and the next hop.

steps.do: Add a static route for a prefix OSPF already provides, and look again.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip route 192.168.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.1
end
show ip route
steps.see: An S entry replaces the O entry for 192.168.30.0/24: a static route's distance, 1, beats OSPF's 110, even though the path is longer.

steps.do: Remove it again, and check the O route comes back.
steps.code:
configure terminal
no ip route 192.168.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.1
end
show ip route

lessons.title: Static, default and floating static routes
objectives: Configure IPv4 and IPv6 static and default routes
Back up a route with a floating static route
Describe what first hop redundancy protocols do
key_points: ip route PREFIX MASK NEXT-HOP sends traffic for a prefix to a next-hop address. Naming only an exit interface is safe on point-to-point links; a fully specified route names both.
A default route, ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 NEXT-HOP, matches every destination that no more specific route does; on an edge router it usually points at the internet provider.

A floating static route has an administrative distance higher than the route it backs up, so it stays out of the table until that route disappears: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.23.2 5 backs up a static default with distance 1.
IPv6 static routes work the same way once ipv6 unicast-routing is on: ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:30::/64 2001:db8:acad:23::2, and ipv6 route ::/0 for a default.
A static route whose next hop can't be reached isn't installed: check with show ip route static and a ping to the next hop.

First hop redundancy protocols (HSRP, VRRP and GLBP) give hosts a virtual default gateway shared by two routers, so the gateway survives a router failure; in HSRP the highest priority (100 by default) is active, and preempt lets it take over again.

walkthrough.title: Back up a default route with a floating static

steps.do: On a router with two links towards the internet, add the primary default route and a floating one with administrative distance 5.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.12.1
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.23.2 5
end

steps.do: See which one is used.
steps.code: show ip route static
steps.see: S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.12.1 only: the floating route waits.

steps.do: Shut down the interface towards 10.0.12.1 and look again.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface g0/1
 shutdown
 end
show ip route static
steps.see: S* 0.0.0.0/0 [5/0] via 10.0.23.2: the backup has taken over.

steps.do: Bring the interface back with no shutdown and check the primary route returns.

lessons.title: Single-area OSPFv2
objectives: Configure single-area OSPFv2 and verify neighbours and routes
Explain router IDs, DR and BDR election, and what stops neighbours forming
key_points: OSPF routers on a link become neighbours by exchanging hellos. Hello and dead timers (10 and 40 seconds on Ethernet), area, subnet and mask, authentication and stub settings must match, and the MTUs must match to reach FULL.

The router ID comes from router-id if it's set, otherwise from the highest loopback address, otherwise from the highest address on an active interface. A new router ID takes effect after clear ip ospf process.

network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 under router ospf 1 runs OSPF on interfaces in that range, and ip ospf 1 area 0 on an interface does it directly. passive-interface stops hellos on LAN interfaces but still advertises their subnets.

On Ethernet, routers elect a DR and a BDR: the highest interface priority wins (1 by default, 0 never takes part), then the highest router ID, and the election isn't pre-emptive. ip ospf network point-to-point on a two-router link skips it.

Cost is the reference bandwidth (100 Mbps by default) divided by the interface bandwidth, so every link of 100 Mbps or more costs 1; auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000, on every router, tells faster links apart.
default-information originate advertises a router's default route into OSPF, and other routers see it as O*E2. show ip ospf neighbor, show ip protocols and show ip ospf interface brief verify OSPF.

walkthrough.title: Bring up OSPF between two routers

steps.do: On R1, start OSPF with a fixed router ID, advertise its networks, and keep hellos off the LAN.
steps.code:
configure terminal
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 passive-interface g0/0
 end

steps.do: On R2, do the same with router ID 2.2.2.2 and its own LAN, 192.168.20.0/24, then check the neighbour.
steps.code: show ip ospf neighbor
steps.see: Neighbour 1.1.1.1 in state FULL/DR or FULL/BDR, on GigabitEthernet0/1.

steps.do: Make the link point-to-point on both routers, so no DR election is needed.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface g0/1
 ip ospf network point-to-point

steps.do: Shut down R2's g0/1 (the link to R1), wait for OSPF to reconverge, and trace again from PC2. Then bring the link back.
The ticket: paste change-r3.txt into R3. Users at site 3 report they can't reach anything. Use the method to find every fault and fix it, recording the commands that showed you each one.

modules.title: Review: IP Services, Security and Automation
modules.summary: The last three domains, reviewed for the exam: the services that keep networks running, the controls that protect them, and how controllers and automation change network management, with a practice lab on an edge router.

lessons.title: IP services: what to configure, verify and recognise
objectives: Recall how to configure and verify NAT, DHCP and NTP
Recognise the roles of DNS, SNMP, syslog, QoS, SSH, TFTP and FTP
key_points: NAT: ip nat inside and ip nat outside must be on the right interfaces, and the access list must match the inside addresses. PAT needs overload; without it, a pool serves only one host per public address.
DHCP: ip helper-address goes on the interface that faces the clients, and the server needs a route back to the relay's address. A router interface becomes a client with ip address dhcp.
NTP: ntp server makes a client, show ntp status should say the clock is synchronised, and the client's stratum is one more than its server's.
Syslog levels 0 to 7 are emergencies, alerts, critical, errors, warnings, notifications, informational and debugging; a configured level includes every level with a lower number.
SNMP agents listen on UDP 161 and traps go to UDP 162; v2c relies on community strings, v3 adds authentication and encryption. TFTP is UDP 69 with no login; FTP uses TCP 20 and 21 and a login.

QoS marks voice EF (DSCP 46) and queues it with LLQ, trusts markings from the edge, polices by dropping excess traffic and shapes by queuing it. SSH needs a host name, a domain name, RSA keys and local or AAA logins.

walkthrough.title: Check an edge router's services in one pass

steps.do: Check NAT: the interfaces, then the translations for current traffic.
steps.code:
show ip nat statistics
show ip nat translations
steps.see: The inside and outside interfaces the right way round, and translations to the outside address.

steps.do: Check DHCP: the leases, and the pool's settings in the configuration.
steps.code:
show ip dhcp binding
show running-config | begin ip dhcp pool

steps.do: Check time and logging.
steps.code:
show ntp status
show logging
steps.see: Clock is synchronized, and the syslog server among the logging destinations.

steps.do: Check management access.
steps.code:
show ip ssh
show running-config | begin line vty
steps.see: SSH Enabled - version 2.0, and transport input ssh on the vty lines.

lessons.title: Security: the exam's favourite traps
objectives: Avoid common mistakes in ACL, port security and DHCP snooping questions
Compare AAA protocols and wireless security options quickly
key_points: ACLs: the first match wins, an unseen deny any ends every list, wildcard masks are inverted subnet masks, standard ACLs go near the destination and extended near the source, and an interface takes one ACL per direction and protocol.
Port security needs the port set to access (or trunk) mode, not left dynamic. Its defaults are one MAC address and the shutdown violation mode, which err-disables the port.
DHCP snooping trusts no port until told to: trust ports towards real DHCP servers and uplinks. Dynamic ARP inspection checks ARP against the snooping bindings, so it depends on DHCP snooping.
TACACS+ uses TCP 49, encrypts the whole message and separates the three As; RADIUS uses UDP 1812 and 1813, encrypts only the password and combines authentication with authorisation.

Wireless: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires Protected Management Frames; Enterprise modes use 802.1X with a RADIUS server. In 2.4 GHz, 1, 6 and 11 are the usual non-overlapping channels.
A vulnerability is a weakness, a threat is what could use it and an exploit is how; IPsec VPNs provide confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay protection.

lessons.title: Automation and programmability
objectives: Compare traditional and controller-based networking
Recognise REST API, JSON, Ansible and Terraform concepts
Explain how AI is used in network operations
key_points: Traditional networks are configured device by device, each with its own control plane. Controller-based networks centralise control and policy in a controller, which talks to applications through northbound APIs and to devices through southbound APIs such as NETCONF, RESTCONF and OpenFlow.
In a software-defined fabric, the underlay is the physical network that provides IP connectivity, and the overlay is the virtual network built on top of it with tunnels such as VXLAN.

REST APIs map HTTP verbs to CRUD: POST creates, GET reads, PUT and PATCH update, DELETE deletes. Status codes in the 200s mean success, 400s a client error (401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found) and 500s a server error.
JSON is built from objects in braces holding "key": value pairs, arrays in square brackets, strings in double quotes, numbers, true, false and null.

Ansible is agentless, pushes configuration over SSH from YAML playbooks, and is idempotent. Terraform describes infrastructure declaratively in HCL, plans changes before applying them and records what it built in a state file.

Predictive AI learns from past data to forecast or flag the unusual, such as traffic anomalies or failing hardware; generative AI produces content, such as configuration drafts or incident summaries, which a person must check before it's used.

lab.title: Services and security on an edge router, then fix them
lab.goal: Give an office edge router DHCP, PAT, NTP, syslog, SSH-only management and a configuration backup, protect the access switch's ports, then find and fix the faults a buggy script introduced.
setup: The starter files r1-base.txt, isp-base.txt and s1-base.txt, the plan in addressing.txt, and change-r1.txt for the ticket at the end

steps.do: Build the topology in addressing.txt and paste the starter files. Give Server0 its static address and turn on its NTP, SYSLOG and TFTP services, and give the Internet server its address.
Make R1 the DHCP server for the office LAN, then set PC1 and PC2 to DHCP.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.20
ip dhcp pool OFFICE
 network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 192.168.1.1
 dns-server 192.168.1.10
 end

steps.do: Configure PAT on g0/1, then ping 198.51.100.10 from both PCs.
steps.code:
configure terminal
access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
interface g0/0
 ip nat inside
 exit
interface g0/1
 ip nat outside
 exit
ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload
end

steps.do: Synchronise R1 to Server0 and send it time-stamped logs.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ntp server 192.168.1.10
service timestamps log datetime msec
logging host 192.168.1.10
end

steps.do: Allow management over SSH version 2 only, from the office LAN only. Answer 2048 for the modulus.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip domain-name example.com
username admin secret Lab-Admin-2026
crypto key generate rsa
ip ssh version 2
access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
 access-class 10 in
 end

steps.do: On S1, turn on port security for the PCs' ports, then ping the gateway from each PC.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface range f0/1 - 2
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 end

steps.do: The ticket: paste change-r1.txt into R1, then connect a new PC3 to S1 f0/3 and set it to DHCP. Users report that nobody can reach the internet and that PC3 has no address. Find every fault with the method, fix it, and check that PC3 gets an address and both PCs reach 198.51.100.10 again.

PAT translates the PCs to R1's outside address.
R1 is synchronised to Server0, and its logs arrive there.
Management is SSH only, from the office LAN only.

R1's configuration is backed up to the TFTP server.
The ticket is solved: the NAT roles are back on the right interfaces and the excluded range no longer covers the pool, each found with a show command.

project.title: Build and troubleshoot a multi-site network
project.brief: Design, build and document a network for a company with a head office and a branch, joined by a WAN link, with internet access at head office. Head office has a staff VLAN and a guest VLAN on two access switches joined by an LACP EtherChannel, running Rapid PVST+ with a chosen root bridge, and a router on a stick. The branch has one LAN. Run single-area OSPFv2 between the sites, with the default route originated at head office. Head office's router is the DHCP server for every LAN, so the branch relays. Hosts reach the internet through PAT, the routers take their time from an NTP server and send it their logs, management is SSH only and only from the staff VLAN, an ACL keeps guests out of the staff VLAN and the branch, and access ports have port security. Give the staff VLAN and the branch LAN IPv6 addresses too, with IPv6 static routes between the sites. When it all works, save a copy, break it with three faults (swap files with a study partner, or use the fault cards provided), and troubleshoot it back to health with the structured method, documenting each fault.
deliverables: An addressing table for IPv4 and IPv6, and a diagram or screenshot of the topology
The running configuration of every router and switch

Verification output: show etherchannel summary, show spanning-tree for the staff VLAN, show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route at both sites, show ipv6 route, show ip nat translations, show ip dhcp binding, show ntp status and show ip ssh
A troubleshooting log for the three faults: the symptom, each step of the method with the commands and output, the cause and the fix
A short reflection: which exam domains felt weakest while you built and fixed the network, and your plan for them

rubric.name: Switching
rubric.description: VLANs, trunks with a non-default native VLAN, a working LACP EtherChannel, the chosen root bridge, and PortFast with BPDU guard on access ports.

rubric.name: Routing
rubric.description: OSPF neighbours are FULL, the routing tables hold every LAN and the O*E2 default, IPv6 static routes connect the IPv6 LANs, and traces show the expected paths.

rubric.name: Services
rubric.description: DHCP works at both sites through the relay, PAT translates inside hosts, and the routers are synchronised by NTP and send logs to the server.

rubric.name: Security
rubric.description: Management is SSH only from the staff VLAN, the ACL keeps guests out of the staff VLAN and the branch without blocking anything else, and access ports have port security.

rubric.name: Verification evidence
rubric.description: Every requested output is included and shows the network working as designed.

rubric.name: Troubleshooting log
rubric.description: Each fault is found with a clear, structured method rather than guessing, with the output that proved the cause and a fix that's verified.

rubric.name: Reflection
rubric.description: An honest view of weak domains, with a specific plan for each.

project.submit: Paste your addressing table, every device's running configuration, the verification outputs, your troubleshooting log and your reflection. If you can share your .pkt files, add links to them.

files.content:
Fault cards for the capstone

When your network works, save a copy of the .pkt file. Then either swap files with a study partner and break each
other's networks, or pick three of these cards at random, apply them to your own copy, and put it away for a day
so you forget which ones you chose. Adapt the commands to your own interfaces, VLANs and addresses.

 1. Move one staff PC's switch port into the guest VLAN.            (switchport access vlan ...)
 2. Remove the staff VLAN from one trunk's allowed list.            (switchport trunk allowed vlan ...)
 3. Set both ends of the EtherChannel to LACP passive.              (channel-group 1 mode passive)
 4. Change the native VLAN at one end of a trunk only.               (switchport trunk native vlan ...)
 5. Give one subinterface the wrong VLAN number.                     (encapsulation dot1Q ...)
 6. Change the OSPF hello interval on one end of the WAN link.       (ip ospf hello-interval ...)
 7. Make the WAN interface passive in OSPF.                          (passive-interface ...)
 8. Remove default-information originate from the head office router.
 9. Remove the ip helper-address from the branch router.
10. Swap ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the head office router.
11. Add a deny statement for the branch LAN near the top of an ACL.
12. Shut down the head office router's WAN interface, then change its description so it looks deliberate.
